title: Supreme Court Lets Border Wall Work Continue in West Texas
summary:
The U.S. Supreme Court said on Monday that work on border barriers in west Texas can move ahead while a court case about the plans continues. The decision clears the way for hundreds of miles of barrier and security work in the Big Bend region, including land inside Big Bend National Park, known for its sweeping canyons and wide, unspoiled desert.

The court's five-page decision was unsigned, meaning no justice signed it as the author. It said the federal judge in El Paso who had paused the work did not have the authority to weigh in. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson was the only justice who disagreed.

The judge's pause had stopped work on 30-foot-tall steel barriers, patrol roads, surveillance systems, and other border infrastructure. The court said federal law lets the Secretary of Homeland Security, Markwayne Mullin, set aside environmental protections and conservation laws to speed up border construction.

The case was brought by the Center for Biological Diversity, an environmental group, a nonprofit working to preserve a historic church near the border. They argued the plans are unconstitutional and that Big Bend residents would be harmed if construction continued.

The plans have drawn criticism from people across the political spectrum. Critics say a wall is not needed in the Big Bend, where rugged land and desert heat already make crossings rare. They worry about the environment, Indigenous sites, wildlife, and tourism.

In its emergency request to the court in late October, the government said a gap in the Big Bend would act as 'a dangerous magnet for cartels and other bad actors.' The Big Bend Sector covers a nearly 500-mile stretch, more than a quarter of the U.S.-Mexico border, and it regularly sees the fewest encounters along the Texas border, according to Customs and Border Protection data.
why_it_matters: The decision shows how courts can shape big building projects, and how protecting nature, keeping borders secure, and respecting local communities can pull in different directions.

background_read: The Supreme Court is the highest court in the United States, and its decisions are the final word on what the law means.
The U.S.-Mexico border is guarded with walls, fences, patrol roads, and cameras, and the government sometimes builds new barriers in places where it thinks people may cross.
Big Bend National Park is a large protected desert park in Texas, known for its canyons and wild land, where building is normally limited to protect nature.
When people disagree about a government plan, they can take the case to court, and a judge can pause the plan while the case is decided.
